# Racial and Ethnic Disparities in Allergen Immunotherapy Prescription for Allergic Rhinitis

**Authors:** Sunjay Modi; Matthew R. Norris; Victoria Nguyen; Robert Bower; Timothy J. Craig; Taha Al-Shaikhly

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Medicine, Section of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology, Penn State College of Medicine, Hershey, Pennsylvania, United States | 2Department of Medicine, Penn State College of Medicine, Hershey, Pennsylvania, United States

## Abstract

Racial and ethnic differences exist in the severity of various atopic diseases including allergic rhinitis (AR). Patients of underrepresented races and ethnicities may be subjected to disparate subcutaneous allergen immunotherapy (SCIT) prescription practices.

To explore the racial and ethnic disparities in the use of SCIT among patients with AR.

In this retrospective matched cohort study, we used the TriNetX US collaborative Network, a multicenter electronic health record-based database to identify AR patients aged 18 years and older. Patients were grouped according to their racial and ethnic identification. Study groups were matched for baseline demographics, atopic comorbidities, heart diseases and utilization of beta-blockers, and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors. The proportion of patients of underrepresented racial/ethnic groups started on SCIT was contrasted to the non-Hispanic White cohort.

We identified 1,038,000 patients with AR, the mean age (±SD) at the index was 49.7 (±16.1) years old, and 64.6% were females. Ethnicity information was available from 87.3% of patients and the majority (92.3%) were non-Hispanic. Over a 3-year observation period, fewer Black patients (RR, 0.40; 95% CI, 0.33 to 0.48) and Hispanic patients (0.80; 95% CI, 0.64 to 0.99) were started on SCIT compared to non-Hispanic White patients. The proportions of Asian who were initiated on SCIT tended to be lower when compared to non-Hispanic White patients (RR, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.47 to 1.009).

In the United States, differences in SCIT prescription exist between Black, and Hispanic patients relative to White patients. Barriers to treatment should be explored and mitigated.

## Abstract

## Introduction

Racial and ethnic disparities in disease severity and treatment practices are evident across the spectrum of the atopic triads, namely asthma, allergic rhinitis (AR), and atopic dermatitis (AD).1 Black and Hispanic patients with asthma are less likely to be maintained on controller therapies and are more likely to seek urgent care treatment for their asthma.1 AD is more prevalent among individuals of underrepresented ethnic and racial backgrounds and additionally suffer more severe and persistent disease.2 Less is known about the racial disparities in AR, but the prevalence of AR is higher among Black and Hispanic individuals.1 Black and Hispanic patients with AR report a lower quality of life.3 Further, racial and ethnic differences in AR phenotypes exist with a higher prevalence of perennial AR with seasonal exacerbations, the phenotype linked to poor asthma control, among Black children and adolescents.4

AR affects 1 in 6 Americans with a considerable impact on quality of life.5, 6 A significant proportion of patients continue to have burdensome symptoms despite pharmacotherapy with intranasal corticosteroids and antihistamines.7 Allergen immunotherapy, primarily administered in the United States via subcutaneous allergen immunotherapy (SCIT), is the only disease-modifying option available for allergic rhinitis. SCIT has consistently been shown to improve quality of life and reduce reliance on daily anti-allergy medications.8 These favorable effects tend to persist after completing the recommended 3–5-year course of SCIT.8 Beyond alleviating AR symptoms, SCIT improves allergic asthma and AD control.9–11 The long-lasting favorable effects of SCIT make it an attractive cost-effective intervention, an important consideration given the tremendous direct and indirect cost of the disease. Previous studies indicated that Black and Hispanic patients endure excessive exposure to indoor allergens, suffer a significant burden from atopic diseases including asthma and AD, and overall experience a lower quality of life from AR.1, 3 Thus, it may be reasonable to anticipate higher pharmacotherapy and SCIT prescription in these underrepresented racial and ethnic groups to alleviate the excessive atopic manifestations. However, a previous study focused on urban-school children with asthma comprised mostly of Hispanic and Black patients showed AR was under-treated as only 1 in 6 children were identified as using an intranasal steroid.12 Information about SCIT prescription among the historically disadvantaged racial and ethnic groups remains limited.

In this study, we leveraged a collaborative network of electronic health records (EHRs) databases from multiple healthcare organizations (HCOs) in the United States (TriNetX US collaborative network, TriNetX LLC, Cambridge, MA), identified adult patients with AR, and then estimated and contrasted the probability of receiving SCIT among the different racial and ethnic groups. Our results provide a snapshot of the real-life racial and ethnic disparities in the SCIT prescription for AR patients.

## Methods

### Data source

The data used in this study was collected on December 19, 2022, from the TriNetX US Collaborative Network, which provided access to electronic medical records (diagnoses, procedures, medications, laboratory values, genomic information) from approximately 93 million patients from 57 HCOs within the United States. TriNetX, LLC is compliant with the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), and any additional data privacy regulations applicable to the contributing HCO. As this study used only de-identified patient records, it was exempted from Institutional Review Board approval.

### Cohort identification and study design

We conducted a retrospective matched cohort study, using the web-based TriNetX live platform. We queried the TriNetX US Collaborative Network for patients with AR aged 18 years and older, seen between January 1, 2010 and December 31, 2018, and had no prior SCIT prescription using the International Classification of Diseases (ICD)-10 codes for AR (J30.1, J30.2, J30.8, J30.9). We excluded patients with Hymenoptera allergy (ICD-10 codes, T63.44, T63.45, T63.46, T63.48) as venom immunotherapy for Hymenoptera allergy shares some of the CPT codes used to indicate SCIT for AR. Meeting the above criteria defined the index event. Patients with AR were grouped into Hispanic and non-Hispanic based on their ethnic identification. We required at least ethnic identification (Hispanic or non-Hispanic) for inclusion in our cohort. Hispanic and non-Hispanic AR patients were further classified based on their racial identification (i.e., White, Black, Asian, and Other Race). Patients identified as Indian-Alaska natives, and Native Hawaiian and other Pacific Islanders were grouped as Other Race. Using the non-Hispanic White patients as our reference standard, we matched study cohorts for baseline characteristics including age, sex, atopic co-morbidities (asthma, asthma severity, and AD), AR type, other co-morbidities or medications that may influence SCIT prescription including heart failure, ischemic heart disease, beta-blocker and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEI) use, and lastly factors that might influence access to healthcare (lower education level and lower socioeconomic status). These diagnoses, medications, and factors that influence access to healthcare were identified within 5 years on or before the index event. After matching, the cohorts were followed for 3 years, and the use of SCIT was identified based on Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) codes (95125, 95120, 95144, 95115, 95117, 95165). To ensure adequate follow-up, we required patients to be living and have a recorded contact with the healthcare system (defined as any of the following: an ICD-10, CPT, or RxNorm code or a visit) on or after December 30, 2021. A complete list of ICD-10 and CPT codes used in the process of cohort identification and study outcome definition is provided in Table E1. We note that in addition to EHR-structured codes, TriNetX generates codes based on machine-reading of clinical notes and documents.

### Statistical analysis

Patient characteristics were described as means and standard deviations (SD)s for continuous variables, and numbers (N) with percentages (%) for categorical variables. To compare baseline characteristics, the t-test and chi-square test were used. For matching, we used 1:1 propensity score matching (PSM). TriNetX generates a propensity score for each patient and uses a “greedy nearest neighbor matching” with a caliper of 0.1 pooled SD to identify matched subsets. To compare SCIT utilization, we estimated and compared the incident proportion over the 3-year observation period between the matched study cohorts. Significance was assessed using the Z-test to compare proportions and the relative risk (RR) and the 95-confidence interval (CI) estimated the direction and magnitude of such interaction. As a confirmatory analysis, Kaplan-Meier survival analysis was used to estimate the probability of initiating SCIT prescription at a daily time interval and accounted for the individuals who exited the cohort during the analysis period whereby patients were removed from the analysis (censored) after the last fact in their record. The significance of the difference in the Kaplan-Meier curves between the groups was assessed using the Log-Rank test. The hazard ratio (HR) and the 95% CI estimated the magnetite and direction of such interaction. TriNetX calculates the HR and its respective 95% CI using the R’s Survival package v3.2–3 and validates results by comparing them with the output from SAS version 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc, Cary, NC). All statistical analyses were performed in real-time using the built-in Compare Cohort feature of TriNetX. Additional graph illustration was performed using GraphPad Prism (version 9, GraphPad Software Inc, San Diego, California).

## Results

We identified 1,038,000 adult patients with AR who met our inclusion criteria. The mean age (±SD) at the index event was 49.7 (±16.1) years old, and the majority (64.6%) were females. Approximately 20% of patients had concomitant asthma. Ethnicity information was available from 906,596 patients (87.3%) and the majority of which (92.3%) were non-Hispanic. Among the non-Hispanic patients with AR, 632,603 (75.6%) patients identified as White, 153,318 (18.3%) as Black and 23,174 (2.8%) as Asian. Race information was unknown from 24,856 (3%) non-Hispanic patients and a small proportion of the non-Hispanic patients (0.4%) belonged to the Other Race group (American Indian/Alaska natives or native Hawaiian and other Pacific Islander). Among the adult Hispanic patients with AR (N = 69,660), 42,728 (61.3%) identified as White, 2,164 (3.1%) as Black and 257 (0.4%) as Asian. Approximately 34% of the Hispanic patients with AR lacked co-racial identification. A flowchart of the cohort construction process is shown in Figure 1. The baseline characteristics of the study groups before PSM are presented in Table E2.

After matching the Black cohort of AR patients to our reference non-Hispanic White cohort, 153,141 patients remained in each cohort and the two cohorts were well-balanced for baseline demographics and atopic co-morbidities (Table 1). During a 3-year observation period, relatively fewer patients (160/153,141) in the Black cohort were started on SCIT as compared to 403/153,141 patients in the non-Hispanic White cohort (RR, 0.40; 95% CI, 0.33 to 0.48; P < .001) (Figure 2A). While statistically non-significant, after 1:1 PSM, the proportion of Asian patients (44/23,173) who was started on SCIT tended to be lower than non-Hispanic White patients (64/23,173) (RR, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.47 to 1.009); P = .054) (Table 2) (Figure 2B). Further survival analysis confirmed the above results with a lower 3-year probability for SCIT initiation among Black relative White patients with AR (HR, 0.40; 95% CI, 0.33 to 0.48) and a trend for lower 3-year probability of initiating SCIT among Asian relative to White patients with AR (HR, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.47 to 1.009) (Figure 2).

During the 3-year observation period, fewer Hispanic patients with AR (N=144/69,656) were prescribed SCIT as compared to matched non-Hispanic White patients (N=181/69,656) (RR, 0.80; 95% CI, 0.64 to 0.99; P =.04) (Table 2) (Figure 3A). As disparities might exist among Hispanic patients based on their co-racial identification, we attempted further matched cohort analyses comparing the Hispanic patients with the various co-racial identification to the non-Hispanic cohort. The baseline characteristics of the Hispanic subgroups are presented in Table E2. We noted lower prescription of SCIT among Hispanic White individuals with AR (79/42,727) when compared to non-Hispanic White patients (108/42,727) (RR, 0.73; 95% CI, 0.55 to 0.98; P = .034; after 1:1 PSM) (Figure 3B). However, no significant difference was noted in the proportion of Hispanic non-White patients started on SCIT when compared to non-Hispanic White (RR, 0.82; 95% CI, 0.59 to 1.14; P =.24). (Figure 3C). Further survival analysis showed similar results with a lower 3-year estimated probability for initiating SCIT among the Hispanic overall (HR, 0.80; 95% CI, 0.64 to 0.99) and the Hispanic White (HR, 0.73; 95% CI, 0.55 to 0.98) relative to non-Hispanic White individuals with AR (Figure 3).

Because TriNetX obfuscates counts that are less than or equal to 10 to ensure the confidentiality of patient data, the small number of patients belonging to the other racial and ethnic groups including non-Hispanic Other Race, Hispanic-black, Hispanic Asian or Hispanic Other Race) limited our ability to conduct further analysis.

## Discussion

To our knowledge, this is the first study to utilize a population-based database and examine the real-life racial and ethnic disparities in SCIT prescription for adult patients with AR. We highlight that SCIT remains an underutilized intervention for treating AR and that significant racial and ethnic disparities in SCIT utilization currently exist with lower prescription of SCIT especially among Black (60% less likely), and to lesser extent Hispanic (20% lower likely) patients with allergic rhinitis when compared to White patients. Our findings might alternatively suggest over-utilization of SCIT among White patients with AR, a hypothesis that would need further investigation. The racial differences in SCIT prescription were evident after controlling for many potential cofounders including age, sex, atopic co-morbidities, heart failure and ischemic heart disease status and was not influenced by the use of beta blockers or ACEIs.

Limited studies have explored the racial differences in SCIT prescription for AR. In other atopic diseases such as asthma, studies have demonstrated fewer Black patients receive controller therapies and Black patients present more often to the emergency department to receive care for acute asthma exacerbation.13 Our finding that there is a lower probability of SCIT prescription among Black patients when compared to White patients extends the disparate practices observed in the treatment of other atopic diseases to allergic rhinitis. This finding is of particular importance as Black patients have higher odds of aeroallergen sensitization when compared to their White counterparts.14 Black individuals also experience a lower quality of life from AR when compared to non-Hispanic White children.3 Further, aeroallergen sensitization is linked to more severe atopic manifestations such as asthma,15, 16 Taken together, one would anticipate higher SCIT prescription in Black patients with AR, which is contrary to our study findings.17 This disparate SCIT prescription that was observed after controlling for age, sex, atopic co-morbidities, and asthma severity calls for allergists to examine and mitigate barriers to SCIT in the Black population with AR.

A previous study focused on Medicaid-enrolled children with AR reported higher prescription of SCIT among Hispanic children but were 1.5 times more likely to discontinue their SCIT when compared to non-Hispanic White patients.18 Hispanic patients with AR experience a lower quality of life from AR when compared to their White counterparts.3 Atopic conditions such as AD and asthma are more pronounced in Hispanic patients and extrapolating these observations to AR, one would similarly anticipate higher SCIT prescription to offset the excessive rhinitis symptoms.2, 19 The use SCIT among Hispanic adult patients with AR relative to White patents varied by the sub-racial groups but was overall less compared to White patients. Interestingly, the lower prescription of SCIT relative to non-Hispanic White among Hispanic patients was noted among White Hispanic and not among non-White Hispanic patients which requires further investigation.

SCIT alleviates symptoms of AD in dust mite sensitized patients, decreases airway hyperresponsiveness to allergen challenge, and improves symptom control in patients with asthma.9, 11, 20 Both conditions can increase the referral likelihood to allergists and may therefore translate into higher prevalence of SCIT among patients with asthma and AD. However, uncontrolled asthma is a recognized risk factor for systemic reactions to SCIT.21 Since the burden of uncontrolled asthma is documented to be higher among Hispanic and Black patients, this could influence SCIT prescription among these patients.1 In this study, we observed lower likelihood of SCIT prescription among individuals of historically disadvantaged ethnic and racial groups after controlling for co-morbid asthma, AD, and asthma severity. The under-utilization of SCIT among Black and Hispanic patients with AR extends a previous study observation in urban school-aged children with asthma, the majority of whom were Hispanic and Black, showed significant undertreatment of allergic rhinitis with less than 25% of patients being treated with intranasal steroids and non-sedating antihistamines.12

Variation in aeroallergen sensitization patterns exists between the Eastern and Western hemispheres.22 House dust mite sensitization is identified in up to 90% of Asian individuals, far greater than in the Western population.17, 22 This may account for the higher disease burden in Asian immigrants with AR.22 A telephonic-based survey that examined the burden of AR among the US and ex-US patients found that 35% of Asian-Pacific patients reported at least a moderate impact of AR on their quality of life, on par with US adults.23 In this study, relatively fewer Asian patients with AR received SCIT as compared to White patients; however, the result was not statistically significant, likely ascribed to the small sample size included in our matched cohort analysis, and thus should be interpreted with caution. We note that in other atopic diseases such as asthma, no difference in biologic prescription was noted suggesting that Asians may be less subjective to disparate care.24, 25

SCIT, a specialized procedure prescribed frequently by allergy specialists, requires frequent in-office administration over a 3–5-year course. Therefore, taking time away from family, work, or school, transportation challenges, and decreased accessibility to allergists, for individuals residing in underserved areas or inequitable referral practices are major barriers. A recent observational study concluded that Black patients are less likely to receive referrals to subspecialists.26 Sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT), which is now approved in the United States, may offer a solution to minimize disparities for those living in underserved areas if not for the lack of insurance approval, may offer a solution to minimize disparities for those living in underserved areas. In a study from Denmark that examined compliance with allergen immunotherapy, authors concluded that SLIT may present an advantage to ensure equitable access to allergen immunotherapy.27

This study was limited by its retrospective design and lack of granular information on the socioeconomic factors that might have accounted for the observed findings, an important area for future study. Nonetheless, a major strength of our study is that we utilized an EHR database from multiple centers that included both publicly and privately insured individuals thereby representing a broad cross-section of the U.S. population. It is noteworthy that while the magnitude of differences identified in our study was small, the overall SCIT prevalence is low, and therefore, such differences can be meaningful.18 Moreover, a greater amount of Hispanic and non-Hispanic Black patients are uninsured and thus the magnitude of racial and ethnic disparities in SCIT prevalence observed in our study may in fact underestimate the actual real-life disparities.28

In conclusion, we used a multicenter EHR-based database and documented significant racial and ethnic disparities in SCIT prescription for AR are evident after controlling for asthma, AD status, asthma severity, allergic rhinitis type, heart disease diagnosis, or utilization of beta-blockers and ACE inhibitors. Our findings extend observations about the existent disparate care in other atopic diseases. Reasons for such disparities can be speculated, but future studies are needed to identify and eliminate barriers to SCIT and ensure equitable care for allergic rhinitis patients of historically disadvantaged ethnic and racial groups.
